n: A second message comes about seven weeks later, during the Feast of Tabernacles (October 520 BC) — the same feast when Solomon had dedicated the first temple.

f.w: the seventh month, in the one and twentieth day
f.g: The last day of the Feast of Tabernacles; about October 17, 520 BC.

n: Again the message is for the governor, the high priest, and all the people.
Some older people remembered Solomon’s glorious temple, destroyed 66 years earlier. Compared to it, this new building seemed like nothing, and they were discouraged.

f.w: Who is left among you that saw this house in her first glory?

n: God’s answer: Be strong, Zerubbabel; be strong, Joshua; be strong, all you people — and work, for I am with you. The same encouragement God gave Joshua of old.
God’s covenant from the Exodus still stands, and His Spirit remains among them. Don’t be afraid.
In a little while God will shake heaven, earth, sea, and land. Hebrews applies this “shaking” to the removal of all that is temporary so the unshakable kingdom remains.

f.w: I will shake the heavens, and the earth

n: He will shake all nations, and their treasures will come in, and He will fill this house with glory. Many Christians read “the desire of all nations” as the Messiah, who came to this temple.

f.g: Hebrew can mean “the treasures of all nations”; many Christians also see it as pointing to Christ.

f.w: I will fill this house with glory

n: The silver and gold belong to God anyway. If He wants the temple beautified, He has the resources.

f.w: The silver is mine, and the gold is mine

n: This later temple’s glory will be greater than Solomon’s, and here God will give peace. The Savior Himself would later teach in this temple (as rebuilt by Herod).

f.w: The glory of this latter house shall be greater
in this place will I give peace

n: A third message comes two months later, in December 520 BC.

f.w: the four and twentieth day of the ninth month

n: Haggai poses a question about the law to the priests, whose job was to teach it.

f.w: Ask now the priests concerning the law

n: If someone carries holy sacrificial meat in a fold of his robe and touches other food, does holiness spread to it? The priests answer, “No.”

f.g: The fold or hem of a garment.

n: But if someone unclean from touching a dead body touches food, does it become unclean? “Yes.” Uncleanness spreads easily; holiness doesn’t transfer by contact.
Haggai’s point: the people themselves had been “unclean” through neglect, so even their offerings were unclean. Rebuilding the altar alone didn’t make them holy; their hearts needed to change.

f.w: that which they offer there is unclean

n: Now think back to how things were before the temple foundation stones were laid.
Back then, a grain heap expected to hold twenty measures held only ten; a wine vat expected to yield fifty measures gave only twenty.
God had struck their crops with blight, mildew, and hail, yet they didn’t turn to Him.
But consider this day — the day the temple foundation was laid again. Things are about to change.

f.w: the foundation of the LORD's temple was laid

n: The seed isn’t even harvested yet, and the trees haven’t borne fruit — but from this day on God will bless them. The promise comes before the evidence; they must trust it.

f.w: from this day will I bless you

n: A fourth message comes the same day, this one just for Zerubbabel.

f.w: the four and twentieth day of the month

n: God will shake the heavens and the earth.

f.w: I will shake the heavens and the earth

n: He will overturn the thrones of kingdoms and destroy their military power; armies will turn on each other — as at the Red Sea and in Gideon’s battle.

f.w: every one by the sword of his brother

n: God chooses Zerubbabel and makes him like a signet ring — a royal seal of authority. This reverses the curse on his grandfather Jehoiachin and keeps David’s line alive; Zerubbabel appears in Jesus’s genealogy.

f.g: A seal ring used to sign official documents — a symbol of royal authority.
